captions.text: Diorite is difficult to carve and highly durable. This ruler of Lagash was made in a stone whose hard surface has preserved the brow and facial features for roughly four thousand years.

This cast reproduces the limestone bust found in the sculptor Thutmose’s workshop at Amarna. Only one eye is inlaid, using quartz and wax; the missing inlay changes the face when viewed from the left.

This small glazed-faience figure combines a lioness’s head with a woman’s body. Its scale differs from the monumental Sekhmet statues familiar from Egyptian temples, showing how the deity was also represented in smaller formats.
Augustus is shown with a raised arm, bare feet, and a narrative breastplate. The small Cupid on a dolphin below his leg refers to divine lineage and also helps support the marble figure.

This Carrara-marble portrait presents Trajan with a plain fringe combed across the forehead rather than elaborate royal regalia. The restrained treatment is part of the visual language of a soldier-emperor.

Authority is carried here by gold and writing. This dinar was struck at Madinat al-Salam, Baghdad, in 290 AH (902–903 CE), during the reign of al-Muktafi. Turn it to compare the inscriptions on both sides. The original coin is only 21 mm across; the separate bar belongs to the recording.
This plaster is after Michelangelo’s Moses for the tomb of Julius II. The horns, tablets, and turned torso identify the figure; the right hand draws the beard aside as the seated body shifts.

Iron, brass, tin, arrows, and cowries have been added to this figure. In Kongo contexts, an nganga could activate nkisi figures in matters such as oaths and disputes; the accumulation of materials is visible around the entire form.
The carved head is fully visible, while the torso is enclosed in cloth and organic material. The construction suggests that the contained materials were integral to the work, not simply a covering.

The Chilean museum identifies this carved stone clava as an insignia of authority. Its broad head, narrow grip, incised lines, and pierced handle give status a form that could be held. Compare these choices with the costume and posture of the figures elsewhere in the exhibition.
This figure combines carved cottonwood with pigment, cotton cloth, tanned leather, and metal. The separate additions are important to its construction and can be identified from different sides.

This late sixth-century brass figure has a single halo that encloses both head and body. The radiating form explains the "combined halo" in its title; changes in light make the raised rays easier to see.
The source links this gowe from Nias to the recognition of social rank. Its frontal pose, enlarged head and emphatic facial features make that status visible.
Authority can be carried by a seat as well as a standing figure. Carved supports and a curved upper surface distinguish this chiefly stool from Cameroon.
A leopard’s head becomes an attachment for ceremonial dress at the court of Benin. The animal image is made portable and wearable in lead and ivory.

power-and-presence.invitation: These works show different ways authority becomes visible. Compare the materials, scale, facial treatment, gesture, inscriptions, and objects that establish rank or carry political and protective meaning in distinct settings.
power-and-presence.coda: Authority can be represented by a figure or carried by an object. Material, pose, inscription, and setting help explain how each work made status visible.
power-and-presence.summary: Across time and place, authority has taken shape in portraits, protective figures, precious materials, inscriptions, and objects made to be held.

sacred-forms.invitation: These works were made for specific religious, ceremonial, commemorative, or protective purposes. Their function, materials, and original settings are central to understanding them; the object records provide the available context.
sacred-forms.coda: A 3D model can clarify form and construction, but it does not replace the original setting, use, or community knowledge attached to a work.

captions.text: The falcon is larger than the king, who stands between its legs. Both figures are carved from metagraywacke and share a continuous polished surface, linking the god and pharaoh in one block of stone.

This is a limestone false door for the priest Iryenakhet, not an opening door. In ancient Egyptian funerary practice, false doors provided a symbolic point through which the deceased could receive offerings; the frontal design supports that use.

Rows of Arabic writing cover this marble tombstone, dated 830 CE and recorded as Egyptian, probably from Fustat. Its inscribed field makes remembrance visible through words. Compare its layout with the false door, while keeping the different religious purposes and historical settings of the two works in mind.
The robe carries carved images of the realms of desire across the chest, shoulders, and back. The program continues around the body, so a single frontal view does not show the whole design.
This Goryeo-period bodhisattva of compassion is made of gilt wood with copper, iron, and crystal elements. Low-angle light helps distinguish the gilding from the inset materials.

Javanese carvers made this figure from andesite, a volcanic stone with a visibly pitted grain. The transition between elephant head and human body is carved as a continuous form rather than a joined assembly.
Made around 1000 CE from guaiacum wood with shell inlay, this figure functions as a stand. Its dense wood and supporting form are central to how the object was made and used.
This helmet mask was worn on top of the head rather than over the face. The hollow underside shows how it was fitted for a dancer’s crown.
Wood, glass, beads, brass tacks, and pigment are combined in this maternity figure. The mother’s arm and the child form the central structural link in the composition.
This is a cast after Michelangelo’s marble Pietà, completed before he was twenty-five. The original is the only work he signed, with the signature placed on the strap across Mary’s chest.

This painted wooden Pietà once hung on the front of a cottage in Chochołów, Poland. The carved figures and their shelter belong together. Compare it with Michelangelo’s Pietà: the shared subject takes a different form in a shrine made for the setting of a home.
Donatello positioned Saint George with weight forward, legs apart, and shield grounded. The stance was designed to be legible from the street below the original niche.
Harihara combines aspects of Shiva and Vishnu in a single body. The arch and surviving attributes help organize the figure even where parts are missing.

The carved seal and its virtual impression show two ways to read the same surface. The impression unfolds a scene of approach to the seated moon god Sin; it is a digital visualization beside the scanned object.
Several episodes from the infancy of Christ share the small ivory field. The plaque was probably part of a treasure binding, joining narrative carving to a precious book cover.

Painted skin and gilded drapery make the martyr’s body vivid against the branching tree. This was a devotional image; its later queer reception is a separate chapter in how Saint Sebastian has been viewed.

Carved after Girona’s plague epidemic, this panel belonged to a larger altarpiece dedicated to Saint Sebastian. Painted flesh and gilded surfaces make his bound body vivid. The isolated panel preserves the central image while the surrounding altarpiece has been lost.

the-work-of-the-surface.invitation: In these works, meaning is often carried by the surface: shallow relief, incised lines, paint, glaze, drill work, and small changes of depth. Use the lighting controls to make those details clearer.
the-work-of-the-surface.coda: Surface is not decoration alone. It can record narrative, status, technique, and the work of making.

captions.text: This gypsum-alabaster relief from the Northwest Palace at Nimrud represents a royal hunt in shallow carving. Low-angle light helps separate details such as reins, bowstrings, and manes.
Carved by a Kongo artist in 1861, this relief follows the taper and curve of the ivory tusk. Its design changes as the curved surface is viewed from different angles.

Closely incised signs follow the curved wooden surface of this Rongorongo tablet from Rapa Nui. The museum records 1,580 glyphs and notes that the writing remains undeciphered. Rotate the tablet to follow the rows around it; seeing the cuts clearly is different from knowing what they say.
This 1904 plaster by Charles Carpeaux records a twelfth- to thirteenth-century naval-battle relief from the Bayon. It preserves the scene through a cast made from an earlier surface.
The Northern Qi carver used the robe as a picture plane, working the realms of desire into the limestone drapery. The imagery is part of the figure’s surface as well as its iconography.
Michelangelo carved this relief while still in his teens. Some figures project strongly from the marble while others remain shallow, and the rough upper edge retains visible tool marks.
This single marble round uses several depths of carving. The Virgin’s head projects almost fully into the round, while the figures behind her are reduced to much shallower forms.
This Quapaw ceramic vessel takes the form of the Underwater Panther, a being in Mississippian belief. The hollow container is integrated into the animal body rather than added as a separate element.
The ornament on this late Shang wine vessel was made through a mold: ridges visible on the bronze began as recessed designs in the casting surface.
This helmet mask has four faces and no single back. Each quarter turn presents a different face, making the work legible from multiple directions.
Overglaze polychromy and gold depict a courtly gathering on stonepaste. The painted figures follow the curved profile of the bowl.

Carved and drilled ivory panels expose gold leaf beneath the casket’s stars and rosettes. Painting was added to the smooth areas in the fifteenth century. Move around the lid and sides to distinguish openings, shallow carving, and painted marks: several kinds of surface work coexist on this small box.
Gold-colored paint, cowries and carved striations organize the face. The source identifies this as a decorative wall piece made in Ghana around 1990, drawing on Luba kifwebe forms.
Black and white triangles follow the chip-carved pattern around the eyes and mouth. Seen from the side, the patterned plane gives way to the projection of the face.
Engraving and openwork make the silver cup intricate; concealed channels also make it difficult to drink from. The embracing eagle and bear turn its support into a second subject.
Brass allows the slender limbs and elaborate hairstyle to stand free of the body. The collection describes a contemporary figure combining Senufo forms and a Fulani hairstyle.
Pevsner builds a curved surface from welded metal filaments. Follow the repeated lines around the form: they define planes and openings without becoming a solid block.
The rough outer skin of the alabaster meets a precisely finished interior. Moving around the block reveals where untouched stone becomes carved architecture and where empty space acquires an edge.

Holes pierce the concrete in the pattern of the constellation Columba. In the original tunnel, daylight carries that pattern onto the interior. This reconstruction isolates one cylinder from Holt’s four-part installation.
The torso emerges from rough, unfinished stone. SMK’s plaster cast preserves that contrast in relief, allowing the viewer to trace the transition between worked anatomy and the surrounding block.

Two women remove their garments in the circular field inside the cup. Tilt the vessel to see how the painted scene follows the shallow bowl, then compare it with the figures on the outside. This digital reconstruction records both image and container; the scene’s precise meaning remains uncertain.

Carved wood, paint, and gilding work together: relief gives the body and tree their depth, while color distinguishes skin, cloth, and setting. Side light reveals a different order of details from the one established by the painted surface.
Rodin places softly modeled bodies above a roughly worked marble base. Move around the pair to compare the smooth backs and shoulders with the ridges of stone beneath them.
Marble folds cling to the figure while gathering into a lifted veil. Rotate the sculpture to follow the contrast between thin drapery and the denser waves below.
The smooth back and shoulders rise from a roughly worked block. Rodin lets the transition between those surfaces remain visible around the seated figure.
Pennies become a perforated skin. Move around the torso to compare the coins’ repeated circles with the continuous curves they construct; the material remains legible even as it describes a body.

Gill compresses two intertwined figures into a narrow stone slab. The shallow carving makes the couple’s contours and the block’s edges part of the same continuous surface; the damaged corner belongs to the surviving sculpture.
The slender bronze turns the torso into an extended contour. Its narrow waist and rounded hips become especially clear as the light moves across the surface.

the-work-of-the-surface.summary: Works show how shallow relief, incised writing, drilled depth, modeled clay, paint, and carved ornament carry information.

bodies-in-motion.invitation: Each work represents a selected moment: a throw, a fall, a step, a struggle, or a turn. Compare how balance, support, and the direction of the body make movement legible from different viewpoints.
bodies-in-motion.coda: Sculpture represents movement through a fixed form. The change of view shows how each artist solved that problem.

captions.text: The original bronze is lost; this version preserves the spiral composition from the trailing toes through the twisted torso to the raised disc. The head is a modern restoration, which affects how the figure is read in the round.

The two wrestlers are carved as an interlocked marble group. From a low viewpoint, the lower figure’s arm can be seen behind his back and the points of contact—knee, hip, and grip—show how weight is distributed.
This small fired-clay dancer is held in the Saint-Raymond reserves and is usually not on public display. The statuette uses the angle of the body and drapery to suggest a step.

Carved for the tomb of Julius II, this figure has only lightly indicated bonds: a thin band across the chest and one arm folded overhead. The pose combines the conventions of captivity, sleep, and release.
This companion figure has arms bound behind the back, a twisted torso, and a turned head. The plaster cast records the worked surface of the marble; low-angle light makes tool marks more apparent.
Laocoön and his sons are arranged on a rising diagonal, with the serpents linking all three bodies. Viewing from the side or back helps trace how each coil connects the group.
Rodin retained the torso and legs while omitting head and arms. Both feet rest flat on the ground, so the sense of walking is constructed from the pose rather than observed from a natural stride.

The lowered gaze, lifted heel, and flowing robe turn a step into an image of calm teaching. Walking Buddhas are characteristic of Sukhothai sculpture in Thailand. Compare this complete figure with Rodin’s Walking Man: each makes a fixed body suggest a different kind of movement.

This figure comes from Le Jeu de l’écharpe, a Sèvres table centerpiece designed for viewing in the round. Unglazed biscuit porcelain keeps the surface matte, while the scarf establishes the direction of movement.

This warrior was designed for the tapering corner of the Aphaia temple’s west pediment. The figure’s propped elbow and extended legs fit the triangular architectural space and were intended to be seen from below.
The Smithsonian lists this work as not on view. Eberle places the child’s weight well beyond her feet, using implied momentum rather than a stable standing balance.
Often misnamed a gladiator, this fighter lunges along a line from rear heel to raised left arm. His upward gaze suggests an opponent above him, probably on horseback.
A lifted arm and a bent leg animate this porcelain faun. The adjacent support and rectangular base allow the twisting body to remain stable.
Lacinová-Jílková gathers several bathers around a central standing figure. Compare the lifted arms and seated bodies as the group turns through space.

Rogiers stretches the figures until reclining begins to resemble dancing or struggling. The branching base participates in their balance. The original is blue; this archive preserves an uncolored model.
A raised palm arrests the movement of a girl clutching a teddy bear. Fenriz uses a clear, open gesture to express resistance and vulnerability in this digital sculpture.
A long taper suggests flight without wings, feet, or feathers. This later digital interpretation follows Brâncuși’s reduction of a bird to an upward movement held in a fixed form.
Hercules must hold Antaeus clear of the earth to defeat him. Turning the group reveals the grips and counterweights that keep two struggling bodies suspended above a small base.

Hermes bends toward his sandal while turning his attention outward. The lifted foot and twisting torso suggest a task interrupted. Move around the figure to see how the support stabilizes the body while the head redirects its movement.

Hercules wrestles Achelous after his rival has taken the form of a serpent. The hero’s bent legs brace the struggle while the coils pull the action in another direction. Different views clarify the grip and the distribution of weight.

The kneeling figure throws both arms upward as its weight sinks. Compare the immense modeled strength of the body with the loss of control suggested by its pose. This bronze was cast in 1961 after a model developed in 1940–1942.
The tilted head, turned torso and bent leg make a continuous curve. Rodin’s deliberate removal of the arms concentrates attention on the body’s balance.
Three dancers turn around a shared center. Follow the linked arms and shifting feet to see how the circle holds together from different sides.
The raised cup, outstretched arm and lifted heel carry the figure into a turning gesture. Drapery gathers around the hips while the upper body opens outward.
A stretch draws the elbows apart and turns the torso. The relaxed pose depends on a precise shift of weight between the planted feet.

A turn travels through the abdomen into the shoulders and hips. This original digital sculpture isolates the torso to make the body’s opposing directions visible without the assistance of a face or gesture.

The suspended step and trailing fabric suggest forward motion. Because this is an original digital sculpture, its precarious balance does not depend on the physical supports required by a carved or cast figure.

Two bodies lean into one another while their extended limbs and sweeping drapery suggest movement through the air. Puttinati gives the lovers from Dante’s poem a shared balance that can be read from several sides.
The dancers hold their faces and upper bodies close while their arms open outward. The sweep of drapery connects their steps and gives the embrace a turning rhythm.
The figure raises both arms into a long, twisting contour. Follow the shift of weight from the feet through the torso and into the lifted hands.
The kneeling figure stretches both arms around her head. Smooth marble and a roughly worked base place the body’s movement against the resistance of the stone.

bodies-in-motion.summary: Works use posture, balance, and composition to describe movement: throwing, falling, wrestling, dancing, and walking.

what-survives.invitation: These works survive through loss, copying, repair, and changes of use. Look for breaks, missing elements, joins, and later additions; each affects what can be known about an object and its history.
what-survives.coda: Survival can involve damage, copying, and alteration. Later additions and careful preservation become part of an object’s history alongside its original making.

captions.text: Probably a seated hero, perhaps Ajax, this work survives as a torso and thighs. The twist between hip and ribcage still indicates the original pose, especially when viewed in the round. Michelangelo studied the torso closely.
This fragment has no known name or date and survives without head or arms. The lightly modeled musculature is one of the few available clues to how the original figure was conceived.

This mammoth-ivory figure was damaged by excavation tools when it was discovered in 1922. The digital model records a mold of the original. Look for the difference between the surviving outline and the damaged surfaces: discovery and later copying have both shaped how the sculpture is encountered.
Phidias’s gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos is lost. This plaster records a later copy associated with Athena’s sanctuary at Pergamon, preserving the design at several removes from the original.

This horse head comes from the team that drew Selene’s moon chariot on the Parthenon’s east pediment. The strained jaw, vein, and flared nostril were designed to read at the low corner of the architectural setting.
Carved in oak around 1430, this is intentionally a head on a platter: the subject is John the Baptist’s beheading. Its partial form belongs to the original design, rather than later damage.

This eagle-headed figure came from the palace walls of Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud. Wing feathers are incised row by row in alabaster; the broken edges show that the relief was once part of a larger wall program.
This head belongs to a Hercules type usually shown resting on a club. Although the body and club are missing here, the downcast gaze still relates to that larger composition.
This giant’s head came from the north side of the Pergamon Altar’s battle of gods and giants. Deep drill channels in the hair create strong contrasts of light and shadow.
This bronze horse head from Herculaneum ends at the neck. Its opening reveals hollow casting: large bronze sculpture is typically formed as a metal shell rather than a solid block.

This cast records an Amarna-period head identified as a queen, possibly Kiya or Meritaten. The museum leaves the sitter’s identity open. Compare the unfinished facial areas and short surviving neck; the cast preserves the small head, while its modern mount supplies a separate support.

This Ottoman fritware jug acquired silver-gilt mounts in London around 1592. The metal covers the rim, handle, and foot and adds a hinged lid. The Fitzwilliam explains that these additions protected fragile edges and made the vessel more luxurious. Look at the joins to follow its changing form.
At only 4.7 cm high, this Neolithic head carries its identity in the eyes, nose and hair. The fragment preserves those choices while leaving the original body and setting uncertain.
Two people remain visible beneath the pediment, but the inscription below them has been lost. The missing text changes what can be known about the people this monument commemorated.
The iron Buddha preserves a Goryeo-period sculptural presence in a material that can corrode and change at the surface. The source dates the figure broadly, from 918 to 1392.
Water levels can reveal or submerge this coil of basalt and earth, while salt alters its surface. The model records one appearance of an artwork whose material setting continues to change.

The missing head and arm belong to the sculpture’s physical history; they are not gaps created by the 3D viewer. The surviving dog, drapery, and stance still help identify Meleager. The fragment shows how much an attribution can depend on what remains beside a body.

An ancient ivy-crowned head has been joined to a modern bust. The mount gives the portrait a complete presentation without restoring its original body. Look at the transition below the neck: the figure now seen is also a record of later collecting and display.
Only the upper portion of this erotic pipe tamper survives. The patinated break belongs to the historical object; the model preserves a fragment rather than supplying its lost lower bodies.

Javier Villar reconstructed Kolbe’s Dawn from photographs. Compare its interpreted surfaces with the direct scans elsewhere: copying preserves a recognizable composition while introducing decisions made by a later modeler.

what-survives.summary: Fragments, casts, damaged objects, and later additions show how discovery, copying, preservation, and changing use shape the works we encounter.

newExhibition.title: The Other Kingdom
newExhibition.kicker: Animals as vessels, guardians, symbols, and performers
newExhibition.summary: Across three thousand years and several regions, these works use animals to carry religious, political, domestic, and ceremonial meanings. They are not a single tradition; each has its own context and purpose.
newExhibition.invitation: Compare what each animal form is made to do. Some contain liquid, guard a place, support a ritual, represent a deity, or carry a rider. The model can help reveal details on the back, underside, and sides of each work.
newExhibition.coda: Animal sculpture can represent more than an animal. Material, function, and setting determine what each figure meant to the people who made and used it.

works.text: A feline and a snake share this ceramic vessel’s body. The stirrup-shaped spout is integrated with the animal form, showing how the potter combined container and image in one structure.
Shang casters covered this bronze wine ewer with masks, dragons, and animal forms. Low-angle light makes the distinctions between raised motifs and the underlying vessel easier to see.
This relief shows a keeper lifting a cage door as a lion runs out. It was made for Ashurbanipal’s palace at Nineveh, where royal hunting scenes represented the king’s control over dangerous animals.
The bronze she-wolf is shown with the twins beneath her. The wolf and the children were made centuries apart, an important example of how a familiar image can combine elements from different dates.
This horse was part of Selene’s moon chariot on the Parthenon’s east pediment. Its bulging eye, flared nostril, and slack jaw were positioned at the lower edge of the composition.
Apis was a living bull selected by priests at Memphis and honored after death. This representation is carved from serpentinite, whose dark surface changes subtly under different lighting.

This lion guarded the temple of Al-Lat at Palmyra, sheltering a gazelle between its forepaws. After the limestone work was damaged in 2015, digital documentation supported a reconstruction later that year.
This small Florida wood carving combines human and panther features. Its survival is notable because wood rarely endures for long periods; the carved details remain visible across the surface.
This guardian lion from the Bayon at Angkor is built with a squared chest, fixed haunches, and a flattened face. Its placement suggests that it was intended to be encountered while moving past it.

This Quapaw vessel represents the Underwater Panther, a being associated with rivers in Mississippian belief. Made around 1500 in clay and pigment, it combines animal imagery with a container for water.
This ram mask was made to be worn. The curled horns sit above openings for a dancer’s eyes; the underside shows the fitting that once rested on a moving human head.
This carousel horse, made around 1917 from basswood, paint, glass, and steel, was designed to carry a rider. As an outside-row horse, one side faced spectators and received more decorative attention.
Short legs support an ample, rounded body. This ceramic dog gives an everyday animal a durable and exaggerated sculptural form; its precise date remains unknown.
The mouse wraps closely around its chestnut, making a compact netsuke. Fur, ears and the nut’s ridged surface reward viewing at a larger scale than the tiny original.
The beaver’s teeth, chewing stick and patterned tail identify an animal within a larger Haida pole. This model records one section rather than the whole pole.

pairings.title: Figures in Motion
pairings.line: Both works use a raised limb and a carefully balanced body to suggest action. They were made about fifteen centuries apart.

pairings.title: Defeat in Sculpture
pairings.line: Both works show defeated warriors supported by one arm. Each was made within a culture that framed the subject through military victory.

pairings.title: Neolithic Contemporaries
pairings.line: Made at roughly the same time in different regions, these works use contrasting materials and approaches: flat marble planes in the Aegean and ridged clay ornament in Jōmon Japan.

pairings.title: Seated Figures
pairings.line: Both works use a compact seated pose. One rests a bronze chin on a knuckled hand; the other draws a terracotta torso inward.

pairings.title: Portraits of Authority
pairings.line: These portraits use symmetry, controlled expression, and idealized features to represent authority across a span of roughly thirteen centuries.

pairings.title: Mother and Child
pairings.line: Made an ocean and four centuries apart, both works use the mother’s body and hands to support and frame a child.

additionalExhibitions.title: The Price of Victory
additionalExhibitions.kicker: War, glory, and the people who pay
additionalExhibitions.summary: These works examine how art turns war into glory—and how wounded bodies, captives and grieving families complicate the story. A journey from ancient battle monuments to a contemporary appeal for children caught in war.
additionalExhibitions.invitation: A battle can appear as an achievement, a spectacle, a humiliation, or a personal loss. Beginning around 500 BCE and ending in 2022, these works ask who is allowed to look heroic and who must carry the cost. Compare the attacking soldier with the captive, the celebrated leader with the wounded body, and the figure of Victory with a frightened child. Look at what each work asks you to admire, whose suffering it makes visible, and whose perspective it leaves outside the frame.
additionalExhibitions.coda: Return to the title of the exhibition. Who gets to name an event a victory? The answer may change when the person speaking is a ruler, a captive, a grieving sibling, or a child trying to keep one small thing safe.

works.text: c. 500–490 BCE. A warrior lies wounded in a figure from the west pediment of the Temple of Aphaia. Isolated from the larger composition, his vulnerable body becomes the center of attention. The exhibition begins here, before a victor is named: what does fighting do to the people whose bodies make a battle possible? This model records a later plaster cast.

113 CE. Roman soldiers attack in a relief from Trajan’s Column, a monument celebrating the emperor’s campaigns in Dacia. Military violence becomes part of a public account of imperial achievement. Compare the troops with the wounded warrior: a collective image of strength can give a different meaning to combat than a single injured body. Atrium shows a scan of a plaster cast.
The Amazon’s wound interrupts an idealized body. A figure remembered for fighting is shown through exposure and injury, placing vulnerability beside the martial identity that makes her recognizable.

600–900. Prisoners stripped of their battle regalia are brought before a Maya lord, contrasting with the elaborately dressed warriors. This cacao vessel probably circulated as a political gift. Victory becomes something to display and exchange: the captives’ humiliation helps establish the authority of the people who commissioned, gave, or received it.

12th–13th-century Khmer relief; plaster cast made in 1904. At Bayon, a naval battle enters the carved narrative of a temple. Compare its setting with Trajan’s column: warfare can become part of the enduring image of a society’s power. This cast carries only a section of that larger account. The surrounding architecture, other scenes and original setting shape how such a battle is read.

Spartacus led resistance to the society that had enslaved him. Foyatier gives the rebel the monumental nude body usually reserved for celebrated heroes. Set beside images of imperial conquest, this figure asks whose struggle receives dignity and whose freedom is treated as a threat.

Modeled c. 1837–1846; carved 1856. Tecumseh led an Indigenous coalition against U.S. expansion. Decades after his death, Pettrich imagined him as a fallen classical hero. The Smithsonian identifies this as a fictive portrait and questions its presentation of conquest as inevitable. A defeated leader can be given a noble image while the continuing significance of his resistance is pushed aside.

Achilles’s anger begins with the loss of Briseis, a captive treated as a prize in the struggle between Greek commanders. Bissen concentrates the drama in the hero’s tense body. The woman at the center of the dispute remains outside the image, reminding us whose experience heroic narratives can omit.

Memorial designed 1906–1908; this marble replica carved 1912–1915. Victory raises a flag and laurel, yet lowers her eyes. French designed the memorial for James Melvin, whose three brothers died in the American Civil War. Triumph and bereavement occupy the same figure. Can a monument honor a victory without making loss seem worth its price?

1989, using a sculpture modeled in 1963–1964. Hrdlicka’s inverted Marsyas forms part of a memorial to victims and opponents of fascism, racism and war. The broken wall and exposed body give public remembrance a language of injury. Here the classical figure carries the burden of twentieth-century violence.

2022. A girl has fled in her nightclothes and tries to protect her teddy bear. Fenriz describes the sculpture as a tribute to children and other civilians caught in war. The person doing the protecting also needs protection. After armies, captives and monuments, this small act changes the measure of courage—and asks whose safety a victory is meant to secure.

additionalExhibitions.title: The Body Under Pressure
additionalExhibitions.summary: Michelangelo and Rodin, in six encounters: twelve sculptures reveal how a shift of weight, a folded limb or a supporting hand can give feeling a physical form.
additionalExhibitions.invitation: A body can be still and full of effort. Across these six pairings, Michelangelo and Rodin turn standing, thinking, struggling and embracing into sculptural events. Rodin’s response to Michelangelo is sometimes documented, as in the relationship between Lorenzo de’ Medici and The Thinker. Elsewhere, the encounter is a curatorial comparison: an invitation to test a resemblance, notice a difference and look again. Follow the hands, the bearing of weight and the spaces between limbs. Each changes what the figure seems capable of doing.
additionalExhibitions.viewingNote: Drag either sculpture to turn it; use Expand for a closer view. The two views are framed independently and are not shown at a shared physical scale. Several models record plaster casts after Michelangelo’s originals; the notes identify these. Each object record retains its source and material information.
additionalExhibitions.coda: The hand beneath Lorenzo’s chin, Mary’s support of Christ and Adam’s downward gesture all make feeling visible through a physical relationship. Across these works, a figure can hold itself together, bear another body or strain against its own form. Return to one pairing and turn both sculptures away from their familiar front views. Does the comparison still hold when a face disappears and only the body remains?

works.text: The sling and stone belong to a particular story, but the pose delays its action. The supporting leg, relaxed knee and sharply turned head pull attention in different directions. Seen from the side, the poised figure feels less settled than its frontal silhouette suggests.

Rodin worked from the living model Auguste Ney. He removed a spear once held in the left hand, leaving the raised arms open to interpretation. Compare that uncertain gesture with David’s specific equipment: a standing nude can carry either a named task or an unresolved state.

The seated duke gathers his attention around a hand brought to his face. Armor, helmet and the enclosing seat give the pose a formal setting. Trace how the bent arm connects the head to the supported body.
works.modelNote: The 3D model comes from SMK’s Royal Cast Collection.

works.text: A hand props the chin, but thought seems to engage the hunched back, bent legs and planted feet as well. The Musée Rodin identifies Michelangelo’s Lorenzo and Carpeaux’s Ugolino among the pose’s sources. Rodin first conceived the figure for The Gates of Hell in 1880; the enlarged version came later.

The arms are drawn behind the torso while the head turns upward. Rotate the figure to follow the disagreement between shoulders, hips and knees. The bonds give this powerful body a limit against which its movement can be read.
works.modelNote: This model records the SMK cast. The original belongs to Michelangelo’s project for the tomb of Julius II.

works.text: The lowered head and downward-pointing hand direct this muscular body toward the ground. The Musée Rodin connects Adam to Michelangelo’s Sistine figures and relates its proposed setting beside The Gates of Hell to the Louvre display of the Slaves. The pairing here focuses on how bodily turns carry tension.
The lowered head, bent back and deeply folded legs draw the body into a compact volume. Look around the sides to see how knees and elbows both close the shape and leave openings through it.
works.modelNote: The model records a plaster cast in SMK’s Royal Cast Collection, after the sculpture in the Hermitage.

works.text: Rodin’s figure folds deeply while turning across itself. The curve of the back and the angles of the limbs keep interrupting a simple outline. Move around it: the torso, knees and head exchange prominence as the viewing angle changes.
works.modelNote: The scan records the Hirshhorn bronze cast; modeling, enlargement and casting dates are distinct.

works.text: Christ’s body lies across Mary’s lap, with its weight carried by her right arm and the broad mass of drapery. The group gives an irreversible loss a stable structure. Follow the hanging arm, then the hand that holds the torso.
works.modelNote: This model records the SMK cast after the Vatican Pietà.

works.text: The two figures turn toward each other, joining at the mouth while hands and seated bodies establish further points of contact. Rodin developed the lovers from Paolo and Francesca in Dante’s Divine Comedy, then exhibited the group independently. Circle behind them to see how the embrace is built.

A torso and bending limbs become legible within a mass that still carries unfinished passages. This cast preserves the changing boundary between body and block. The rough areas record a different stage of carving; their survival alone does not establish why work stopped.
works.modelNote: SMK’s 2002 plaster cast records the form of the unfinished marble original, not its original stone surface.

works.text: Rodin assembled the torso and legs from studies related to Saint John the Baptist. Without a head or arms, the leaning trunk and separated legs still make a stride intelligible. The fragment is presented as a sculpture in its own right.

comparisons.title: Before the movement
comparisons.summary: Both figures stand with their weight shifted and an arm raised. David’s alert turn and Rodin’s lifted head give the same basic arrangement very different possibilities. One pairing opens a question that runs through the exhibition: how can a still body suggest what has just happened, or what might happen next?
comparisons.lookFor: Compare the supporting leg, the angle of the pelvis and the direction of the head. Then look at what each raised hand is doing.

sources.title: Musée Rodin · The Age of Bronze

comparisons.title: Thinking with the body
comparisons.summary: Here the connection is documented: the Musée Rodin names Michelangelo’s seated Lorenzo as one source for The Thinker. Both bring a hand to the face. Compare what surrounds that familiar gesture: a clothed, contained figure and a nude body whose effort remains visible from head to foot.
comparisons.lookFor: Follow the line from chin to hand, elbow and knee. Turn both figures to see how much work their backs do in sustaining the pose.

sources.title: Musée Rodin · The Thinker and its sources

comparisons.title: A turn becomes a struggle
comparisons.summary: Twisting breaks the body’s alignment. Michelangelo’s captive turns against the restraint of his arms; Rodin’s Adam bends his head and directs a hand toward the earth. Their strength remains visible, yet neither pose reads as effortless. This comparison follows tension through the figure without treating the two subjects as the same story.
comparisons.lookFor: View both from behind. Compare the shoulder line with the pelvis, then follow the change of direction up the spine.

sources.title: SMK · Cast after the Rebellious Slave

comparisons.title: The folded figure
comparisons.summary: A crouch brings distant parts of the body together: head approaches knees, torso meets thighs, and limbs become a surrounding frame. These figures ask to be seen from several sides. What first looks like a closed mass opens into a network of gaps, crossings and unexpected angles.
comparisons.lookFor: Start at the back, then turn toward the lowered head. Compare the empty spaces inside each pose as carefully as the solid forms.

comparisons.title: The weight of another
comparisons.summary: Mourning and desire give these joined bodies different meanings. Their construction creates another conversation: each sculptor must make two figures share support, space and a continuous outline. Compare the one-sided weight of the Pietà with the responsive turns of The Kiss.
comparisons.lookFor: Trace every point where one body touches the other. Which contacts carry weight, which direct movement, and which carry the emotional force of the scene?

comparisons.title: Where does a body end?
comparisons.summary: Michelangelo’s unfinished carving and Rodin’s assembled fragment give incompleteness different histories. In the Captive, the boundary between figure and block remains visible. In The Walking Man, separate studies become a figure that needs neither head nor arms to convey movement. What must be present for a body to feel convincing?
comparisons.lookFor: Compare the figure’s lower edge and the way each leg meets its support. Then look at what the missing or unresolved parts allow the remaining body to express.
